(a) **Enantiomers vs Diastereomers:**

| Feature | Enantiomers | Diastereomers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | Non-superimposable mirror images | Stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other |
| Symmetry | Chiral molecules | Can be chiral or achiral |
| Physical Properties | Identical (except optical rotation) | Different melting points, boiling points, solubility |
| Example | $(+)$-lactic acid and $(-)$-lactic acid | cis-2-butene and trans-2-butene |

(b) **Optical Activity:**
It is the ability of certain chiral substances to rotate the plane of polarization of plane-polarized light (PPL) passing through them.

**Polarimeter Principle:**
Ordinary light passes through a Nicol prism (polarizer) to yield plane-polarized light. This PPL passes through a sample tube containing the optically active solution. The chiral molecules rotate the plane of polarization by an angle $\alpha$. The analyzing Nicol prism is rotated until maximum light transmission is achieved, and the rotation angle $\alpha$ is measured on a graduated scale.
proTip: Remember that diastereomers include both cis-trans (geometric) isomers and compounds with multiple chiral centers where only some configurations differ.
